learning_activity_name: Describe the conceptual framework of accounting (objectives of general-purpose financial statements, users and qualitative characteristics of useful accounting information)
sla_name: The conceptual framework of accounting
sla_method: Internet and library search and Group discussion
sla_assessment_criteria: The conceptual framework of accounting is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of financial statements Financial reports Sample of conceptual framework of accounting
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The conceptual framework is the set of concepts that guides the preparation of general-purpose financial statements. It tells accountants why financial information is prepared, for whom and what makes it useful.
sla_notes_details: The objective of general-purpose financial reporting is to provide information about the reporting entity that is useful to existing and potential investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions about providing resources to the entity. The primary users are these capital providers, while other users include management, employees, customers, suppliers, government agencies such as the Tanzania Revenue Authority and the public. The qualitative characteristics of useful information are fundamental (relevance, which includes predictive and confirmatory value and materiality, and faithful representation, which means complete, neutral and free from error) and enhancing (comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability). The framework also defines the elements of financial statements: an asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events; a liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource; equity is the residual interest; income is an increase in economic benefits and expenses are decreases. Underlying assumptions include the going concern (the entity will continue operating), and constraints include cost and benefit.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trader records a stock of goods at cost because it can be verified from invoices (verifiability) and includes all sales for the year whether cash or credit (completeness) so that the profit shown is a faithful representation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Bank loan officers, investors and the tax authority use financial statements to decide whether to lend, invest or assess tax, and they rely on the qualities described in the framework.
sla_exercise: State the objective of general-purpose financial statements.::To provide financial information about the entity that is useful to investors, lenders and other creditors in making decisions about providing resources.||Name the two fundamental qualitative characteristics.::Relevance and faithful representation.||Define an asset according to the conceptual framework.::A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events.||Give two enhancing qualitative characteristics.::Comparability and understandability (also verifiability or timeliness).

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in the accounting for inventories (meaning, types, valuation methods, stock estimation and insurance claims)
sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for inventories
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of inventories are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of inventories documents
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Inventories are goods held for sale or used in production. Correct accounting for inventories is important because it directly affects cost of sales and profit.
sla_notes_details: Inventories include merchandise for resale, raw materials, work in progress, finished goods and consumable supplies. Under IAS 2 inventories are measured at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV), where NRV is the estimated selling price less costs of completion and sale. Cost includes purchase price, import duties, transport inwards and other costs of bringing goods to their present condition and location. The valuation methods are First In First Out (FIFO), Last In First Out (LIFO, not accepted by IAS 2 but used for study purposes) and weighted average cost (AVCO). Records may be kept using the perpetual system (continuous updating) or the periodic system (counting at the end of a period). Stock may be estimated when it cannot be counted, for example after a fire, by using the gross profit method: closing stock = opening stock + purchases - cost of sales, where cost of sales = sales less gross profit. For insurance claims the amount recoverable is the lower of the value of stock destroyed and the sum insured, subject to any average clause.
sla_notes_illustrations: Opening stock 60 000, purchases 340 000, sales 450 000 and a mark-up of 25% on cost: cost of sales = 450 000/1.25 = 360 000; goods available = 400 000; estimated closing stock = 400 000 - 360 000 = 40 000. If this stock was destroyed by fire and the sum insured was 50 000 the claim is 40 000.
sla_notes_daily_life: Shops count stock at month end, supermarkets use barcode systems to keep perpetual records, and businesses that suffer fire or theft make insurance claims based on estimated stock.
sla_exercise: At what value are inventories measured under IAS 2?::At the lower of cost and net realisable value.||An item cost 800 and can be sold for 750 with no selling costs. At what value is it stated?::At 750, the net realisable value, because it is lower than cost.||Name the three cost-flow methods used to value inventories.::FIFO, LIFO and weighted average cost.||Sales 450 000, mark-up 25%, opening stock 60 000, purchases 340 000. Estimate the closing stock.::Cost of sales 360 000, so closing stock = 400 000 - 360 000 = 40 000.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in the accounting of payroll (meaning, forms and methods of employees’ remuneration and deductions)
sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for payroll
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of payroll are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Payroll
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Payroll is the record of employees' remuneration, deductions and net pay for a period. Accounting for payroll ensures employees are paid correctly and statutory amounts are remitted.
sla_notes_details: Remuneration takes several forms: wages, salaries, overtime, commission, bonuses, allowances and benefits in kind. Methods of remuneration include the time rate (per hour, day or month), piece rate (per unit produced), commission on sales and bonus or profit-sharing schemes. Gross pay is total earnings before deductions. Statutory deductions include Pay As You Earn (PAYE) income tax and the employee's contribution to the pension fund such as NSSF, and other deductions include loan repayments, savings and union dues. Net pay = gross pay - total deductions. Employers also bear costs such as their contribution to the pension fund, the Skills Development Levy and workers' compensation contributions, which are expenses of the employer. A payroll is prepared for each pay period, checked, approved and paid by bank transfer or cash, and payslips are issued to employees.
sla_notes_illustrations: An employee with gross pay of 600 000 has an NSSF deduction of 60 000, assumed PAYE of 50 000 and a loan repayment of 40 000. Net pay = 600 000 - 60 000 - 50 000 - 40 000 = 450 000.
sla_notes_daily_life: Every employee receives a payslip showing earnings and deductions, and employers must deposit PAYE and pension contributions with the relevant institutions each month.
sla_exercise: Define gross pay.::The total earnings of an employee before any deductions.||Name two statutory deductions from wages.::PAYE income tax and the employee's pension fund contribution (NSSF).||Gross pay is 600 000; deductions are 60 000, 50 000 and 40 000. Find net pay.::600 000 - 150 000 = 450 000.||Differentiate time rate from piece rate.::Time rate pays for hours or days worked, while piece rate pays for each unit produced.

sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of investments are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample Bank statement Sample of Business plan Certificate of incorporation
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An investment is an asset held to earn income such as interest and dividends or to gain from increase in value. Accounting for investments requires understanding their types and key terms.
sla_notes_details: Types of investments are equity investments (shares in companies), debt investments (debentures, corporate bonds, government treasury bills and bonds), property investments, fixed deposits and other financial assets. They may be short-term (held for less than a year) or long-term. Important terminologies: a dividend is a share of profit paid to shareholders; interest is the return on loans and debentures; cum-dividend means the buyer will receive the coming dividend and ex-dividend means the seller keeps it; cost of investment includes purchase price and brokerage or stamp duty; a bonus issue is free shares given to existing shareholders in proportion to holdings; a rights issue offers shares to existing shareholders at a discount; capital gain or loss is the difference between selling and carrying value; and the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange (DSE) is the market where listed shares trade. Investments are recorded at cost and later measured at fair value or amortised cost depending on classification.
sla_notes_illustrations: A company holds 1 000 shares of par value 500 shillings and receives a 10% dividend: dividend = 1 000 x 500 x 10% = 50 000 shillings.
sla_notes_daily_life: Individuals buy treasury bills and DSE shares, and cooperative societies invest in fixed deposits, earning interest and dividends that supplement their income.
sla_exercise: Name two types of investments.::Equity investments (shares) and debt investments (bonds or debentures).||What does ex-dividend mean?::The buyer of the share does not receive the forthcoming dividend, which stays with the seller.||Find the dividend on 1 000 shares of 500 shillings each at 10%.::1 000 x 500 x 0.10 = 50 000 shillings.||What is a bonus issue?::Free additional shares given to existing shareholders in proportion to their holdings.

sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for businesses with branches
sla_method: Case studies and Internet and library search
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of businesses operating with branches are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Business licence Sample Branches billboards
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A branch is a part of a business located in another place that sells the goods of the head office. Accounting for branches allows management to know the results of each branch.
sla_notes_details: Branches may be dependent or independent. A dependent branch does not keep full books: goods are supplied by the head office, usually at cost or at invoice (selling) price, sales are made in cash or on credit and cash is remitted to the head office, so the head office keeps the records. An independent branch keeps its own complete books, buys some of its goods on its own, and has its own profit and loss; the head office keeps a branch account (a current account) and the branch keeps a head office account, which must agree after adjusting for goods in transit and cash in transit. Methods for dependent branches include the debtors system, stock and debtors system, final accounts (branch trading and profit and loss) and the wholesale branch system. Goods sent at invoice price include a loading that must be removed to find true profit. Transactions involved are goods sent to branch, returns, cash remitted, branch expenses, discounts and depreciation.
sla_notes_illustrations: A head office sends goods that cost 600 000 to a branch and invoices them at cost plus 25%, which is 750 000. The loading of 150 000 is not profit and is removed in the branch adjustment account.
sla_notes_daily_life: Banks, supermarkets and telecommunication companies have branches in many towns and the head office needs separate results to decide which branches to expand or close.
sla_exercise: Differentiate a dependent branch from an independent branch.::A dependent branch is supplied by head office and does not keep full books, while an independent branch keeps its own full books.||Why is a branch account needed at head office?::To record transactions with the branch and determine its profit or loss.||Goods costing 600 000 are invoiced at cost plus 25%. What is the invoice price and the loading?::Invoice price 750 000 and loading 150 000.||Name two differences that occur when reconciling head office and branch accounts.::Goods in transit and cash in transit.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in the accounting of royalties (meaning, types and terminologies)
sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for royalties
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of royalties are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of royalty agreement Sample of copyrights or trademarks
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A royalty is a payment made for the right to use property such as a mine, patent, copyright or trademark. The payment depends on the extent of use, such as production or sales.
sla_notes_details: The owner of the right is the lessor (or landlord) and the person using it is the lessee. Royalties are calculated as an amount per unit of output or a percentage of sales. Types include mineral royalties (mines and quarries), patent royalties, copyright royalties (books and music), trademark and franchise royalties. Terminology: minimum rent (dead rent or fixed rent) is the least amount the lessee must pay even when the royalty earned is smaller; short workings is the shortfall of royalty below the minimum rent; recoupment is the right to recover short workings from later excess royalty; ground rent is a fixed rent for the land; and a sub-lease exists when the lessee lets part of the property to another person. Royalty agreements usually state the rate, the minimum rent, the period for recouping short workings and the payment dates.
sla_notes_illustrations: Royalty is 2 shillings per tonne mined with a minimum rent of 10 000. When 3 000 tonnes are mined the royalty is 6 000, which is below the minimum rent of 10 000, so the short workings are 4 000.
sla_notes_daily_life: Musicians and authors receive royalties for each copy sold, mining companies pay the government royalties on minerals, and franchise restaurants pay trademark royalties.
sla_exercise: Who is the lessor in a royalty agreement?::The owner of the property or right who receives the royalties.||Define short workings.::The excess of minimum rent over the royalty actually earned in the period.||Royalty is 2 shillings per tonne, minimum rent 10 000, output 3 000 tonnes. Find the short workings.::Royalty = 6 000 so short workings = 10 000 - 6 000 = 4 000.||Give two examples of royalties.::Payments for minerals extracted and payments to authors for books sold (or patent and franchise payments).

sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for non-current assets
sla_method: Internet and library search and Problem solving
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of non- current assets are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of long-term Investments|Land|Property|Plant|Equipment (PP &E) Sample of Trademarks
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Non-current assets are resources held for use over more than one accounting period rather than for sale. Accounting for them includes measurement, depreciation and disposal.
sla_notes_details: Types are property, plant and equipment (land, buildings, machinery, vehicles, furniture), intangible assets (patents, trademarks, goodwill and software) and long-term investments. Initial measurement is at cost, which includes the purchase price, import duties, transport, installation and legal fees, less discounts. After recognition an entity may use the cost model (cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment) or the revaluation model (fair value less later depreciation). Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount over the useful life. Methods are straight line: (cost - residual value)/useful life; reducing balance: a fixed percentage of the carrying amount; and units of production. Factors affecting depreciation are cost, residual value, useful life and method. On disposal a profit or loss arises equal to proceeds less carrying amount (net book value). Depreciation is required by the accruals and matching concepts.
sla_notes_illustrations: A machine costs 1 200 000 with a residual value of 200 000 and a life of 5 years: straight line depreciation is (1 200 000 - 200 000)/5 = 200 000 per year. At 20% reducing balance on 1 000 000 the depreciation is 200 000 in year 1 and 160 000 in year 2.
sla_notes_daily_life: Vehicles lose value with use, so a business shows their reduced book value each year; when it sells an old vehicle for more or less than book value it records a gain or loss.
sla_exercise: Define depreciation.::The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of an asset over its useful life.||Compute annual straight-line depreciation: cost 1 200 000, residual 200 000, life 5 years.::(1 200 000 - 200 000)/5 = 200 000.||Depreciation is 20% reducing balance on 1 000 000. Find the year 2 charge.::Year 1 is 200 000, carrying amount 800 000, year 2 is 160 000.||Name two intangible non-current assets.::Patents and trademarks (or goodwill or software).

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in the accounting of hire purchases (meaning, nature and terminologies)
sla_name: Concepts and principles of accounting for hire purchase
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in accounting of hire purchases.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of hire purchases agreement Sample of goods
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Hire purchase is an arrangement in which a buyer takes possession of goods and pays by instalments, with ownership passing after the last payment. Both the seller and the buyer must account for the transaction.
sla_notes_details: Under a hire purchase agreement the hire vendor (seller) delivers the goods to the hire purchaser (buyer), who pays a deposit and regular instalments. Ownership passes only after the final instalment (and option to purchase fee, if any), so the hire vendor can repossess goods if the buyer defaults. Terminologies: cash price is the price if paid immediately; hire purchase price = deposit + total instalments; hire purchase interest = hire purchase price - cash price; instalment is a periodic payment that includes interest and part of the cash price; and repossession is taking back the goods after default. Differences from credit sale: in credit sale ownership passes at once, while in hire purchase it passes on the final payment. Features are the written agreement, possession before ownership, and the interest charge. Advantages are that buyers acquire assets without paying the full price immediately.
sla_notes_illustrations: A machine has a cash price of 900 000. The buyer pays a deposit of 300 000 and six monthly instalments of 120 000. Hire purchase price = 300 000 + 720 000 = 1 020 000; interest = 1 020 000 - 900 000 = 120 000.
sla_notes_daily_life: Buying furniture, motorcycles or electronics by monthly instalments where the shop keeps ownership until the last instalment is a common example of hire purchase.
sla_exercise: When does ownership pass in a hire purchase agreement?::After the last instalment (and option fee) has been paid.||Deposit 300 000, six instalments of 120 000, cash price 900 000. Find the hire purchase interest.::Hire purchase price 1 020 000 less cash price 900 000 = 120 000.||What can the hire vendor do if the buyer defaults?::Repossess the goods.||Give one difference between hire purchase and credit sale.::In credit sale ownership passes immediately, while in hire purchase it passes after the last instalment.

learning_activity_name: Describe how to develop an accounting action plan
sla_name: Describing how to develop an accounting action plan
sla_method: Internet and library search and Think-ink pair share
sla_assessment_criteria: The steps of developing an accounting action plan are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of action plan Sample of work plan
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An accounting action plan sets out the tasks, people, time and resources needed to keep accounting records and prepare reports. It helps an accountant to work in an organised way.
sla_notes_details: An action plan is a document that lists what must be done, by whom, when and with what resources so that objectives are achieved. Steps in developing it are: (1) set objectives, for example to close the books and prepare monthly financial statements; (2) list the activities such as recording transactions, bank reconciliation, payroll, reconciling ledgers, adjusting entries and preparing the statements; (3) assign responsibility to individuals; (4) set time schedules and deadlines; (5) identify resources such as stationery, software and money; (6) set performance indicators and (7) monitor, review and update the plan. Its contents include the objective, activity, responsible person, time frame, resources, expected output and status or remarks. A good plan is realistic, specific, measurable and flexible, and it supports control and accountability.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a school business club, the objective 'prepare monthly accounts' has activities: week 1 record cash sales, week 2 update ledgers, week 3 prepare trial balance and bank reconciliation, week 4 prepare statements and present to the club.
sla_notes_daily_life: Household budgeting, planning a business's month-end tasks and preparing an audit file are everyday uses of action plans.
sla_exercise: Define an accounting action plan.::A document showing accounting tasks to be done, by whom, when and with what resources.||List four contents of an action plan.::Objective, activity, responsible person, time frame (also resources and expected output).||Why should an action plan be reviewed regularly?::To check progress, correct problems and update it to changing conditions.||Name two accounting activities that could be included in a monthly plan.::Bank reconciliation and preparing the trial balance (or recording transactions or payroll).

sla_name: Developing an accounting action plan
sla_assessment_criteria: An Accounting action plan is well developed.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of accounting|Action plans
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: In this activity students prepare an actual accounting action plan, for example for their business club. They apply the steps to produce a clear table.
sla_notes_details: To develop a plan, begin by gathering information about the business activities and reporting deadlines. Write the objective in a measurable form, such as prepare monthly income statement and statement of financial position by the 5th day of the next month. Break it into tasks and arrange them in order. For each task state the responsible person, start and end dates, resources and expected result. Estimate time and cost realistically and add a column for status or comments. Consider risks such as late receipts of documents and add measures. Present the plan in a table with columns for serial number, activity, person responsible, time, resources, and output, and share it with the team. During implementation record what was actually done and compare with the plan.
sla_notes_illustrations: A club plan: 1. Record daily sales - treasurer - daily - cash book - up-to-date cash book; 2. Petty cash count - secretary - weekly - vouchers - petty cash balanced; 3. Trial balance - accountant - 28th of each month - ledgers - trial balance agreed.
sla_notes_daily_life: The same skill is used when a small business owner schedules payments to suppliers, tax returns and stock counts for the year.
sla_exercise: Why should an objective in the plan be measurable?::So that progress can be checked and it is clear when the objective has been achieved.||Name the columns of a simple action plan table.::Activity, responsible person, time frame, resources and expected output.||What should be done if a task is delayed?::Record the reason, revise the schedule and take corrective action.||Give an example of an activity that should be done daily in a small business.::Recording sales and payments in the cash book.

learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to inventories (using: different stock- taking systems (perpetual and periodic) and using different inventory valuation methods (FIFO, LIFO and weighted average))
sla_name: Recording inventory under FIFO, LIFO and weighted average
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to inventories, are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of inventories documents
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students prepare accounting records for inventory using the perpetual and periodic stock-taking systems and different inventory valuation methods.
sla_notes_details: Under the perpetual system a running balance of inventory is updated after every purchase and sale using a stores ledger card, while under the periodic system inventory is counted physically at the end of the period and cost of sales is found by deducting closing stock from goods available for sale. Three valuation methods are commonly used: First-In-First-Out (FIFO) assumes the earliest units bought are the first ones sold, so closing stock is valued at the most recent purchase prices; Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) assumes the most recently bought units are sold first, so closing stock reflects older, usually lower, prices; the weighted average method recalculates a new average cost per unit after every purchase or once at the end of the period by dividing total cost of goods available by total units available, and uses that average to value both sales and closing stock.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trader buys 100 units at Tsh 2,000 and later 100 units at Tsh 2,400; after selling 120 units, FIFO values the 80 remaining units at Tsh 2,400 each (Tsh 192,000), LIFO values them using the earlier price of Tsh 2,000 each (Tsh 160,000), and the weighted average method values them at the average cost of Tsh 2,200 each (Tsh 176,000).
sla_notes_daily_life: A shopkeeper who buys the same product at different prices over the months must choose a consistent method to value the goods still on the shelves when preparing accounts for the bank or the tax authority.
sla_exercise: Under which stock-taking system is a running balance of inventory maintained after every transaction?::The perpetual inventory system.||Which inventory valuation method assumes that the units bought first are sold first?::The First-In-First-Out (FIFO) method.||How is the weighted average cost per unit calculated?::By dividing the total cost of goods available for sale by the total number of units available for sale.||Why might a business record higher profit when using FIFO during a period of rising prices?::Because FIFO values closing stock at the most recent, higher prices, which lowers the cost of sales charged against revenue.

learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to payroll (computations of gross pay and net pay, payroll summary for remunerations and deductions, and journal entries)
sla_name: Recording payroll transactions
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to payroll, are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Payroll
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students learn how gross pay, deductions and net pay are computed and recorded through a payroll summary and journal entries.
sla_notes_details: Gross pay is an employee's total earnings before any deductions, made up of basic salary plus allowances, overtime and bonuses. From gross pay, statutory and other deductions are subtracted, such as Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) income tax, the employee's contribution to the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) or PSSSF, health insurance (NHIF) and any loan repayments or union dues, to arrive at net pay, the amount actually paid to the employee. A payroll summary lists every employee's gross pay, each deduction and the net pay for the period, and totals each column. In the ledger, the journal entry debits salaries and wages expense with total gross pay, credits the relevant liability accounts for each deduction withheld and credits the bank or cash account with the total net pay actually disbursed; the employer's own statutory contributions are recorded as an additional expense and a corresponding liability.
sla_notes_illustrations: An employee earns a gross salary of Tsh 800,000; PAYE of Tsh 60,000 and NSSF employee contribution of Tsh 80,000 are deducted, giving net pay of Tsh 660,000. The journal entry debits Salaries Expense Tsh 800,000 and credits PAYE Payable Tsh 60,000, NSSF Payable Tsh 80,000 and Bank Tsh 660,000.
sla_notes_daily_life: Every organisation that employs staff, from a small retail shop to a government office, must compute and record payroll correctly each month to pay workers accurately and remit statutory deductions to the relevant authorities on time.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?::Gross pay is total earnings before deductions, while net pay is the amount remaining after all deductions have been subtracted.||Name two statutory deductions commonly withheld from an employee's salary in Tanzania.::Pay-As-You-Earn (PAYE) income tax and the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) contribution.||What does the payroll journal entry credit when net pay is paid to employees?::The bank or cash account, for the total net pay disbursed.||Why are PAYE and NSSF deductions recorded as liabilities rather than expenses when withheld?::Because the amounts withheld from employees still belong to the tax authority or the fund and must be remitted, so they represent amounts the employer owes until paid over.

sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students record the acquisition and disposal of shares bought as investments and account for the returns earned on them.
sla_notes_details: Shares of other companies may be bought as an investment either cum-dividend, where the price includes a dividend about to be paid so part of the price paid is treated as investment income receivable and deducted from cost, or ex-dividend, where the quoted price excludes the forthcoming dividend so the whole price is capitalised as cost. On acquisition, the Investment in Shares account is debited with the cost (price paid plus brokerage) and Bank is credited. When shares are sold, the account is credited with the carrying cost of the shares disposed of, Bank is debited with the sale proceeds, and any difference is recorded as a profit or loss on disposal. Dividends received are recorded as investment income in the income statement, while proceeds from a rights issue taken up or renounced are treated as an addition to, or reduction of, the cost of the investment.
sla_notes_illustrations: A company buys 1,000 shares cum-dividend at Tsh 1,050 each when a dividend of Tsh 50 per share is due; Tsh 50,000 is credited to dividend receivable and the remaining Tsh 1,000,000 is debited to Investment in Shares. When the shares are later sold at Tsh 1,200 each, Bank is debited with Tsh 1,200,000, Investment in Shares is credited with Tsh 1,000,000 and Tsh 200,000 is recorded as profit on disposal.
sla_notes_daily_life: A family business that buys shares on the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange to earn dividends and grow its savings needs accurate records of what was paid, what was received as dividends, and what was gained or lost when the shares were eventually sold.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between buying shares cum-dividend and ex-dividend?::A cum-dividend price includes a dividend soon to be paid, part of which is deducted from cost, while an ex-dividend price excludes the dividend and is capitalised in full as cost.||How is profit or loss on disposal of shares calculated?::By comparing the sale proceeds received with the carrying cost of the shares that were sold.||Where are dividends received on an equity investment recorded?::As investment income in the income statement.||Why does brokerage or commission paid when buying shares form part of the cost of the investment?::Because it is a direct cost incurred to acquire the asset and so is added to the purchase price to arrive at total cost.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to businesses operating with branches (ledger accounts for dependent and independent branches)
sla_name: Accounting for business branches
sla_method: Internet and library search and Problem solving
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to businesses operating with branches are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Business licence Sample Branches billboards
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students prepare ledger accounts for branches that depend on head office for goods and cash, and for branches that keep their own complete records.
sla_notes_details: A dependent branch does not keep a full set of books; head office maintains a Branch Stock Account, a Branch Debtors Account and a Branch Adjustment or Branch Profit and Loss Account in its own books to record goods sent to the branch, goods returned, cash remitted, and to determine the branch's profit, often using goods invoiced at selling price so that loading for profit can be removed in the adjustment account. An independent branch keeps its own complete set of books including a Head Office Current Account, and periodically sends copies of its trial balance to head office, which maintains a corresponding Branch Current Account; the two current accounts must show equal and opposite balances once in-transit items are reconciled, and on combining the accounts inter-company balances are cancelled to prepare combined financial statements.
sla_notes_illustrations: Head office sends goods costing Tsh 500,000 to a dependent branch, invoiced at Tsh 650,000, a mark-up of Tsh 150,000. The Branch Stock Account is debited with Tsh 650,000, and the loading of Tsh 150,000 is later removed through the Branch Adjustment Account so that only the real profit is reported.
sla_notes_daily_life: A trading company that opens outlets in different towns needs a system to track what goods and cash each branch has received from head office and how much profit each branch is really making.
sla_exercise: What is the main difference between a dependent branch and an independent branch?::A dependent branch does not keep its own complete set of books while an independent branch does, including its own Head Office Current Account.||Why are goods sent to a dependent branch sometimes invoiced at selling price instead of cost?::To allow head office to control the branch's stock and prevent theft or loss by comparing expected sales value with actual sales.||What account in the branch's books corresponds to the Branch Current Account kept by head office?::The Head Office Current Account.||What must be true of the balances on the Head Office Current Account and the Branch Current Account before combined accounts are prepared?::They must agree, showing equal and opposite balances, once any items in transit are accounted for.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to royalties (in the books of the lessor and lessee when the contract provides minimum rent and when it does not provide minimum rent)
sla_name: Accounting for royalties
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to royalties are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of royalty agreement Sample of copyrights or trademarks
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students record royalty transactions in the books of the lessor and the lessee, including situations with and without a minimum rent.
sla_notes_details: A royalty is a payment made by a lessee to a lessor for the right to use an asset such as a mine, patent or copyright, usually based on output or sales. Where a lease provides for a minimum rent, also called dead rent, the lessee must pay at least that fixed amount even if the actual royalty calculated from output is lower; the difference between minimum rent and the actual royalty earned is called short workings, which the lessee may be allowed to recover from royalties in excess of minimum rent in later years, subject to a recoupment period stated in the agreement. In the lessee's books, Royalties Account is debited with the actual royalty and Short Workings Account is debited with any shortfall, while the Landlord's Account is credited with the minimum rent; in the lessor's books the entries are reversed.
sla_notes_illustrations: A mining lease sets a minimum rent of Tsh 4,000,000 per year and a royalty of Tsh 200 per tonne extracted. In a year when only 15,000 tonnes are extracted, the royalty earned is Tsh 3,000,000, so short workings of Tsh 1,000,000 arise and the lessee still pays the lessor Tsh 4,000,000.
sla_notes_daily_life: A company that leases land from the government to extract minerals or sand must keep accurate royalty records to pay the correct amount and to know how much short workings it may later recover.
sla_exercise: What is meant by minimum rent in a royalty agreement?::The least amount the lessee must pay the lessor in a period even if the royalty calculated from actual output is lower.||How are short workings calculated?::By subtracting the actual royalty earned from the minimum rent for the period.||What is the purpose of a recoupment clause in a royalty agreement?::It allows the lessee to recover short workings paid in earlier years from royalties that exceed minimum rent in later years, within an agreed period.||In the lessee's books, which account is credited with the minimum rent payable?::The Landlord's (Lessor's) Account.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to non-current assets (valuation, depreciation and disposal)
sla_name: Accounting for non-current assets
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to non-current assets are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of long-term Investments|Land|Property|Plant|Equipment (PP &E) Samples of Trademarks
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students value non-current assets, compute depreciation and record the disposal of assets that are sold, scrapped or exchanged.
sla_notes_details: A non-current asset is initially recorded at cost, which includes its purchase price plus any costs necessary to bring it to its location and working condition, such as installation and delivery. Depreciation spreads this cost, less any estimated residual value, over the asset's useful life; the straight-line method charges an equal amount each year, while the reducing balance method charges a fixed percentage of the asset's remaining net book value each year, giving higher charges in early years. On disposal, the asset's cost and accumulated depreciation are removed from the ledger, the sale proceeds are recorded, and the difference between net book value and proceeds is recognised as a profit or loss on disposal in the income statement.
sla_notes_illustrations: A machine costing Tsh 20,000,000 with an estimated residual value of Tsh 2,000,000 and a useful life of 6 years is depreciated on the straight-line basis at Tsh 3,000,000 per year. If it is sold after 4 years, when accumulated depreciation is Tsh 12,000,000, its net book value is Tsh 8,000,000; selling it for Tsh 9,500,000 gives a profit on disposal of Tsh 1,500,000.
sla_notes_daily_life: A transport company that owns a fleet of buses must depreciate them correctly each year and account properly for any bus that is later sold or scrapped, so that its financial statements reflect the true value of its assets.
sla_exercise: What items are included in the cost of a non-current asset besides its purchase price?::Costs necessary to bring the asset to its location and working condition, such as delivery and installation costs.||How does the reducing balance method of depreciation differ from the straight-line method?::The reducing balance method charges a fixed percentage of the asset's remaining net book value each year, giving decreasing charges over time, while the straight-line method charges an equal amount every year.||How is profit or loss on disposal of a non-current asset calculated?::By comparing the sale proceeds with the asset's net book value at the date of disposal.||What is meant by the residual value of a non-current asset?::The estimated amount the asset could be sold for at the end of its useful life.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records related to hire purchases (in the books of hire vendors and hire purchasers)
sla_name: Accounting for hire purchase transactions
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to hire purchases are appropriately prepared and maintained.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of hire purchases agreement Sample of goods
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students record hire purchase transactions in the books of both the hire vendor (seller) and the hire purchaser (buyer).
sla_notes_details: Under a hire purchase agreement, the buyer takes possession of goods and pays a deposit followed by instalments that include both a repayment of the cash price and interest, but ownership passes to the buyer only after the final instalment is paid. In the hire purchaser's books, the asset is recorded at its cash price and depreciated normally, while the interest element of each instalment is charged separately to the income statement as a finance cost, using the total interest and either the straight-line or actuarial method to apportion interest between periods. In the hire vendor's books, the transaction is treated as a sale on credit for the cash price, with the interest charged over the term of the agreement recognised as income as it is earned.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trader buys equipment on hire purchase with a cash price of Tsh 6,000,000, a deposit of Tsh 1,000,000 and total interest of Tsh 800,000 spread over four equal instalments. The equipment is recorded in the buyer's books at the cash price of Tsh 6,000,000 and depreciated, while the Tsh 800,000 interest is charged to the income statement over the four periods as it accrues.
sla_notes_daily_life: A small business that acquires a delivery vehicle or machinery on hire purchase because it cannot pay the full price at once needs correct records to separate the real cost of the asset from the interest it is paying for the credit.
sla_exercise: What is the key feature that distinguishes a hire purchase agreement from an outright cash sale?::Ownership of the goods passes to the buyer only after the final instalment has been paid, even though the buyer takes possession earlier.||At what value is a hire purchase asset recorded in the buyer's books?::At its cash price, excluding the interest charge.||How is the interest on a hire purchase agreement treated in the buyer's income statement?::It is charged as a finance cost, spread over the term of the agreement rather than recorded all at once.||How does the hire vendor treat the sale of goods under a hire purchase agreement?::As a sale at the cash price, with the interest earned recognised as income gradually over the term of the agreement.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Evaluate the impact of using different inventory valuation methods on reported profits/ losses and the financial position of a business
sla_name: Evaluating the impact of inventory valuation methods
sla_assessment_criteria: The impact of using different inventory valuation methods on reported profit/loss and financial position of a business are logically evaluated.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of company evaluation policy Sample of Income Statements Sample of Statement of financial position
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students compare how FIFO, LIFO and weighted average affect the profit and the financial position reported by a business.
sla_notes_details: The choice of inventory valuation method changes the value placed on closing stock, which directly changes cost of sales and therefore gross and net profit, and also changes the value of inventory shown as a current asset in the statement of financial position. During a period of rising prices, FIFO gives a lower cost of sales and therefore higher reported profit and a higher stock value; LIFO gives a higher cost of sales, lower reported profit, and a lower, less up-to-date stock value; the weighted average method produces results between these two extremes. Because profit differs by method, the choice affects tax payable and comparability between businesses, which is why accounting standards require a business to apply its chosen method consistently from period to period.
sla_notes_illustrations: Using a trader with 80 remaining units, FIFO reports the highest closing stock value of Tsh 192,000 and therefore the lowest cost of sales and highest profit, LIFO reports the lowest closing stock value of Tsh 160,000 and the highest cost of sales and lowest profit, while the weighted average value of Tsh 176,000 falls in between.
sla_notes_daily_life: A business owner deciding which valuation method to adopt should understand that the choice can make the same trading activity look more or less profitable, which affects decisions such as how much tax is paid or how attractive the business looks to a lender.
sla_exercise: During a period of rising prices, which inventory valuation method tends to report the highest profit, and why?::FIFO, because it values closing stock at the most recent higher prices, lowering the cost of sales charged against revenue.||How does the choice of inventory valuation method affect the statement of financial position?::It changes the value at which closing inventory, a current asset, is reported, which in turn affects total current assets and net assets.||Why does the weighted average method usually give profit figures between those of FIFO and LIFO?::Because it uses an average cost that blends both older and more recent purchase prices rather than using either extreme.||Why must a business apply its chosen inventory valuation method consistently over time?::So that financial statements from one period to the next remain comparable and are not distorted by switching methods to manipulate reported profit.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Perform relevant computations to correct various accounting errors using a suspense account
sla_name: Correcting errors using a suspense account
sla_assessment_criteria: Computations to correct various accounting errors using a suspense account are correctly performed.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of suspense account
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students perform computations to locate and correct accounting errors that cause a trial balance not to balance, using a suspense account.
sla_notes_details: When a trial balance fails to balance, the difference is temporarily posted to a Suspense Account so that the final accounts can still be drafted while the cause of the imbalance is investigated. Errors that cause an imbalance include errors of one-sided entry, where an amount is posted to only one account, errors of transposition where digits are reversed in one figure, errors of casting or addition, and errors of omission of one entry of a double entry. Once located, a correcting journal entry is made that debits or credits the account that was wrongly stated and completes the double entry through the Suspense Account, and once all identified errors are corrected the Suspense Account balance should reduce to nil.
sla_notes_illustrations: A trial balance shows a shortage of Tsh 9,000 on the debit side, which is posted to a Suspense Account. Investigation finds that a purchase of Tsh 9,000 was correctly recorded in the Purchases Account but omitted from the Creditor's Account; the correcting entry credits Creditor's Account Tsh 9,000 and debits Suspense Account Tsh 9,000, clearing the suspense balance.
sla_notes_daily_life: A bookkeeper who finds that the totals of a shop's trial balance do not agree at month end uses a suspense account so that the accounts can proceed while the exact mistake is traced and corrected.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of opening a Suspense Account?::To temporarily record the difference on a trial balance that does not balance, so work can continue while the cause of the error is investigated.||Give an example of an error that would cause a trial balance to disagree.::An error of one-sided entry, where an amount is posted to only one of the two accounts required by double entry.||What is a transposition error?::An error where the digits of a figure are reversed or rearranged when it is recorded, such as writing Tsh 4,500 instead of Tsh 5,400.||What should the balance on the Suspense Account be once all the errors causing it have been found and corrected?::Nil, because the correcting entries clear the suspense balance completely.

main_competence_name: Preparing accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Analyse the impact of various accounting errors (commission, principle, original entry and transposition) on the reported profit/loss and the financial position of a business
sla_name: Analysing the effect of accounting errors on profit and financial position
sla_assessment_criteria: The impact of various accounting errors in the reported profit/loss and the financial position of a business is logically analysed.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Income Statements Sample of Statement of financial position
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students analyse how errors of commission, principle, original entry and transposition affect the profit or loss and the financial position reported by a business.
sla_notes_details: An error of commission occurs when a transaction is entered in the correct class of account but in the wrong personal account, for example charging one customer's account instead of another; this does not affect the trial balance but misstates individual account balances. An error of principle occurs when a transaction is recorded against the fundamental rules of accounting, such as treating a capital expenditure as a revenue expense, which understates assets and understates profit. An error of original entry happens when the wrong amount is entered in both the debit and credit accounts, so the trial balance still balances but both accounts are misstated by the same wrong amount. A transposition error, where digits of a figure are reversed in only one account, is normally revealed by the trial balance disagreeing, but if a similar error occurs in the opposite direction in another account the errors may compensate and leave the trial balance unaffected. In each case, correcting the error may increase or decrease reported profit and change the value of assets, liabilities or capital shown in the statement of financial position.
sla_notes_illustrations: A business buys office furniture for Tsh 2,000,000 but records it as a repairs expense, an error of principle. This overstates expenses by Tsh 2,000,000, understating profit by the same amount, and understates non-current assets by Tsh 2,000,000; correcting it increases profit and increases assets by Tsh 2,000,000.
sla_notes_daily_life: An accountant reviewing a company's books before submitting annual financial statements checks for such errors because they can make a business look less profitable or less valuable than it actually is.
sla_exercise: What is an error of principle, and give an example?::It occurs when a transaction breaks a fundamental accounting rule, such as recording the purchase of a non-current asset (capital expenditure) as an ordinary expense.||Why does an error of commission not cause the trial balance to disagree?::Because the amount is still posted as a debit and a credit of equal value, only to the wrong personal account, so both sides of the trial balance remain equal.||What effect does wrongly treating a capital expenditure as a revenue expense have on reported profit?::It overstates expenses and therefore understates the reported profit for the period.||What is an error of original entry?::An error where the wrong amount, often taken from a misread source document, is entered correctly on both the debit and credit side, so the trial balance still balances.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in preparing records and financial statements relating to dissolution and amalgamation of partnerships (meaning, reasons/causes, procedures and realisation)
sla_name: Concepts of partnership dissolution and amalgamation
sla_method: Scenario and Internet and library search
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in preparing records and financial statements relating to companies, dissolution and amalgamation of partnership firms are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Chart with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) Sample of Partnership agreement Sample of Dissolution of partnership deed Sample of profit share agreement
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students describe the meaning, causes and procedures for the dissolution and amalgamation of partnership firms.
sla_notes_details: Dissolution of a partnership is the process of winding up the firm's affairs, ending the partnership relationship among all partners, by realising the firm's assets, paying off its liabilities and outside creditors in full, then repaying partners' loans, and finally distributing any remaining balance among the partners according to their capital and profit-sharing ratios; common causes include the death, retirement or bankruptcy of a partner, expiry of an agreed term, mutual agreement, or the firm becoming unable to carry on its business lawfully. Amalgamation occurs when two or more existing partnership firms combine to form a new firm, so that the old firms are dissolved and a new set of books is opened for the combined entity; this requires revaluing the assets and liabilities of the old firms to agreed values, settling the amounts due to or from partners of the old firms, and recording the assets and liabilities taken over at their agreed values in the new firm's books.
sla_notes_illustrations: Two small partnership firms, each running a retail shop, agree to combine into a single larger firm. Before amalgamation, each firm's assets and liabilities are revalued to current fair values, a Realisation Account is used to record the transfer, and the new firm opens its books with the agreed values of assets, liabilities and partners' new capital balances.
sla_notes_daily_life: When business partners decide to stop trading together, or when two family businesses decide to join forces to compete better, they must follow proper accounting procedures to fairly settle what each partner is owed.
sla_exercise: What is meant by dissolution of a partnership?::The winding up of a partnership firm's affairs by realising its assets, paying off liabilities and distributing any balance among the partners.||Give two reasons why a partnership might be dissolved.::The death or retirement of a partner, or the expiry of a fixed term agreed for the partnership.||What is amalgamation of partnership firms?::The combining of two or more existing partnership firms into a new firm, requiring the old firms to be dissolved and a new set of books opened.||In what order are amounts paid out when a partnership is dissolved?::Outside creditors and liabilities are paid first, then partners' loans, and finally any remaining balance is distributed to partners according to their capital and profit-sharing ratios.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles applied in preparing records and financial statements relating to companies (meaning, types, reserves, retained earnings, dividends and procedures for raising share capital)
sla_name: Concepts of company accounts and share capital
sla_method: Brainstorming and Internet and library search
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles applied in preparing records and financial statements relating to companies are clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of financial statements Sample of share capital
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students describe the meaning and types of companies, and how companies build reserves, declare dividends and raise share capital.
sla_notes_details: A company is a business entity with a legal identity separate from its owners, commonly classified as a private limited company, whose shares are not offered to the public, or a public limited company, whose shares may be bought and sold on a stock exchange. Companies raise share capital either through a private placement to selected investors or through a public issue of shares, which may be issued at par, or at a premium above nominal value credited to a Share Premium account. Reserves are amounts set aside from profit to strengthen the company, such as a general reserve built up for future needs or a statutory reserve required by law, while retained earnings represent accumulated profits not yet distributed to shareholders. Dividends are the portion of profit distributed to shareholders, usually declared as an amount per share by the directors, and may be paid as an interim dividend during the year or a final dividend after the year end.
sla_notes_illustrations: A company issues 500,000 ordinary shares of Tsh 1,000 par value at Tsh 1,200 each. Bank is debited with Tsh 600,000,000, Share Capital is credited with Tsh 500,000,000 and Share Premium is credited with Tsh 100,000,000; if the directors later declare a dividend of Tsh 50 per share, total dividends of Tsh 25,000,000 are declared.
sla_notes_daily_life: Anyone who buys shares in a company listed on the Dar es Salaam Stock Exchange should understand how the company raises capital and decides on dividends, since this affects the returns an investor receives.
sla_exercise: What is the main difference between a private limited company and a public limited company?::A public limited company may offer its shares to the public and have them traded on a stock exchange, while a private limited company's shares are not offered to the public.||What account is credited when shares are issued at a price above their par value?::The Share Premium account, with the excess of the issue price over the par value.||What is the difference between a reserve and retained earnings?::A reserve is an amount specifically set aside from profit for a stated purpose, while retained earnings are the general accumulated profits not yet distributed or transferred to a specific reserve.||What is the difference between an interim dividend and a final dividend?::An interim dividend is declared and paid during the financial year, while a final dividend is declared after the year end, based on the year's results.

learning_activity_name: Describe the concepts and principles of cost and management accounting (Cost accounting: meaning, importance and classification of costs; Cost-Volume-Profit model: meaning, assumptions and limitations, contribution margin and break-even point; Budgeting: meaning, objectives and types)
sla_name: Concepts of cost accounting, CVP analysis and budgeting
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles relating to the use of cost and management accounting i.e., cost accounting, CVP model and budgeting are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of budget Sample of fixed cost|Variable cost|Direct cost|Indirect cost
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students describe cost accounting, the Cost-Volume-Profit model and budgeting as tools of management accounting.
sla_notes_details: Cost accounting is the process of recording, classifying and analysing the costs of producing goods or services so that management can control costs and make decisions; costs are classified by behaviour into fixed costs, which do not change with output, and variable costs, which change directly with output, and by traceability into direct costs, traceable to a specific product, and indirect costs or overheads, shared across products. The Cost-Volume-Profit (CVP) model examines how changes in costs, selling price and sales volume affect profit, using the concept of contribution, selling price minus variable cost per unit, to find the break-even point, the level of sales at which total contribution exactly covers fixed costs and profit is zero. Budgeting is the process of preparing a formal financial plan for a future period; its objectives include planning operations in advance, coordinating the activities of different departments, communicating targets, motivating staff and providing a basis for controlling performance by comparing actual results against the budget.
sla_notes_illustrations: A product sells for Tsh 5,000 with variable cost of Tsh 3,000 per unit, giving a contribution of Tsh 2,000 per unit; if fixed costs are Tsh 4,000,000 per month, the break-even point is 4,000,000 divided by 2,000, which is 2,000 units per month.
sla_notes_daily_life: A small manufacturer deciding how many units of a product to produce and at what price uses cost classification and the break-even point to know the minimum sales needed to avoid a loss, and prepares a budget to plan cash needs for the coming months.
sla_exercise: What is the difference between a fixed cost and a variable cost?::A fixed cost stays the same regardless of the level of output, while a variable cost changes in direct proportion to the level of output.||How is contribution per unit calculated?::By subtracting the variable cost per unit from the selling price per unit.||What is meant by the break-even point?::The level of sales at which total contribution exactly equals fixed costs, so that the business makes neither a profit nor a loss.||Give two objectives of preparing a budget.::To plan and coordinate future activities, and to provide a basis for controlling performance by comparing actual results with the budgeted figures.

sla_name: Analysing and interpreting financial statements
sla_method: Internet and library search and Group discussions
sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts and principles relating to analysis and interpretation of financial statements are properly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Samples of financial statements

sla_notes_intro: Students describe the meaning, objectives, techniques and categories of ratios used to analyse and interpret financial statements, along with their limitations.
sla_notes_details: Analysis and interpretation of financial statements is the process of examining a company's financial statements to assess its performance, financial position and prospects, with objectives that include helping investors decide whether to invest, helping lenders assess creditworthiness, and helping management identify strengths and weaknesses. Common techniques include ratio analysis, comparing figures over time and comparing figures between businesses. Ratios are grouped into categories: profitability ratios such as gross and net profit margin measure how well a business turns sales into profit; liquidity ratios such as the current ratio and quick ratio measure the ability to meet short-term obligations; efficiency ratios such as inventory turnover and debtors' collection period measure how well assets are used; and gearing ratios such as the debt-to-equity ratio measure reliance on borrowed funds. Limitations of ratio analysis include that it relies on historical data that may not predict the future and can be distorted by different accounting policies between businesses.
sla_notes_illustrations: A business with a current ratio of 2:1 appears able to cover its current liabilities twice over from its current assets, but if most of those current assets are slow-moving inventory rather than cash or debtors, the quick ratio, which excludes inventory, may reveal a less comfortable liquidity position.
sla_notes_daily_life: A bank manager deciding whether to lend money to a business, or a supplier deciding whether to offer credit, uses ratio analysis on the business's financial statements to judge whether it is profitable enough and liquid enough to be a safe customer.
sla_exercise: Name the four broad categories of financial ratios.::Profitability ratios, liquidity ratios, efficiency ratios and gearing (leverage) ratios.||What does the current ratio measure?::The ability of a business to meet its short-term (current) liabilities using its current assets.||Give one limitation of using ratio analysis to assess a business.::It is based on historical financial data, which may not reflect current conditions or predict future performance.||Why might two businesses with the same current ratio have different actual liquidity positions?::Because the current ratio does not show the composition of current assets, and one business may hold more cash while another holds mostly slow-moving inventory.

main_competence_name: Prepare accounting reports
learning_activity_name: Prepare and maintain accounting records and financial statements relating to dissolution and amalgamation of partnerships (accounts and statements before and after dissolution and amalgamation)
sla_name: Preparing accounts for partnership dissolution and amalgamation
sla_assessment_criteria: Accounting records relating to companies, dissolution and amalgamation of partnership firms are properly maintained and their relevant financial statements are correctly prepared.
sla_teaching_aids: Sample of Partnership agreement Sample of Dissolution of partnership deed Sample of profit share agreement
sla_references: TET(2023), ACCOUNTANCY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION FORM V-VI, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students prepare the ledger accounts and financial statements needed when a partnership is dissolved or when partnership firms amalgamate.
sla_notes_details: When a partnership is dissolved, a Realisation Account is opened to record the transfer of all assets, except cash and bank, at book value, the sale proceeds of those assets, and the settlement of liabilities not taken over by a partner; any profit or loss on realisation is transferred to the partners' capital accounts in their profit-sharing ratio. Partners' capital accounts are then adjusted for any assets taken over personally, remaining loans are repaid, and a Cash or Bank Account is prepared to show how the final cash is distributed to partners. For amalgamation, each old firm prepares a Realisation Account to close its books, assets and liabilities are transferred to the new firm at agreed, often revalued, figures, and the new firm opens a fresh set of books recording the assets and liabilities taken over and the partners' opening capital balances.
sla_notes_illustrations: On dissolving a partnership, assets with a book value of Tsh 30,000,000 are sold for Tsh 34,000,000, giving a profit on realisation of Tsh 4,000,000 which is shared between two partners in their agreed 3:2 ratio, adding Tsh 2,400,000 and Tsh 1,600,000 respectively to their capital accounts before the final cash distribution.
sla_notes_daily_life: When family business partners finally decide to close their partnership and go their separate ways, or two shopkeepers decide to merge their businesses, these accounts ensure each partner receives a fair and correctly calculated share of what is owed to them.
sla_exercise: What is the purpose of the Realisation Account when a partnership is dissolved?::To record the sale of the firm's assets and the settlement of its liabilities, and to determine the profit or loss on realisation.||In what ratio is profit or loss on realisation shared among partners?::In their agreed profit-sharing ratio.||What happens to a partner's capital account if that partner takes over an asset of the firm personally?::The partner's capital account is debited with the agreed value of the asset taken over.||When two partnership firms amalgamate, what must be done to their assets and liabilities before they are recorded in the new firm's books?::They must be revalued and agreed upon by all the partners involved before being taken over into the new firm's books.
